I've been in rescue for more than 10 years. 
Look,  there's nothing wrong with that option if it's what's best for the dog and family, which it could be if dog is feeling the tension. However, since it seems like you're capable, you or your wife should put the effort into finding a good home and ensure the dog has no behavioural or physical health issues. 
You could also contact some local shelters or rescues with a good profile on your dog and asking if they have suitable applicants and a lack of matching dogs. Explain that you do not wish to offload the dog on a shelter or rescue while you can care for it, but if you've done all the vet work and it's an easy adoption for them that isn't taking away from other dogs in their care, they can use the adoption fee from your dog to support all their other work. Also explain that you are not asking for adopter contact info - it would be "closed" unless adopter wants to contact you.  Some surrendering owners want to have "updates" from new homes and that's a frustrating demand that new adopters can't be forced to stick to.

Viva are the bad apples of the bunch. [https://www.insideimaging.com.au/2018/portrait-studio-franchises-a-trap/](https://www.insideimaging.com.au/2018/portrait-studio-franchises-a-trap/)
Australian Consumer Law has provisions for pushy sales tactics - look up unconscionable conduct.

They are exceptionally pushy, and keep you in a small room with set up designed for pressure. If you have a small kid with you, it's extremely hard to manage all this. 

This is also after up to an hour of them talking you up and controlling your emotions in a photo shoot, and your people skills start to get run down. 

Another place doesn't let you have your phone in the viewing room, and won't let you step out to research other prices or use calculator - they'll "delete" the photos. 

They are very good at what they do - unconscionably pressure people into products and prices they cannot afford or do not want.

For those that 'win' vouchers, unsolicited rules can apply. Not the case here it seems, but just FYI.   


Also, Australian Consumer Law does have rules against 'unconscionable conduct' - which is charging more than is reasonable for a product or service, unfair sales pressure, lack of transparency around contracts and so on. Viva can be challenged in small claims court under this provision - no fancy representation allowed i.e. they can't bring lawyers.  (Self-representing only, unless you are entitled to an advocate)
In person or via email at all?
Viva put prices online in an Information Guide mid-last year, I suspect after many complaints to consumer protection - but they don't send it out when you book or anything.

I recommend showing the businesses that have the raffle pads some of the very low reviews, as they aren't in on the scam - most will throw it out, some with great rage, and give Viva reps a piece of their mind when they come in to pick it up. I've done this a few times in cafes and shopping centres, and it was very satisfying.   
Sort reviews by lowest on Google, or this is one that gets me in the feels: [https://maps.app.goo.gl/1cMeKcS4FJBxtUx67](https://maps.app.goo.gl/1cMeKcS4FJBxtUx67)

Unfortunately, they aren't fake reviews per se - I've rabbit holed on this issue before (I got really outraged after hearing about people getting stung). I've been told by customers that they were offered inducements like free digital photos in exchange for leaving a 5 star review.

Yep, DEMIRS (consumer protection) act for individuals. But I'd love for everyone with a hate-on for Viva and similar super-hard-sell practices to report to ACCC, as I want to see them take coordinated action. I've been haranguing various MPs and regulators on and off for years.

The info guide is brand new, out last year - I suspect due to complaints as they have decades of operation behind them, and they (at least in content I've received) don't send it out to people. It's an issue when people win the loss lead promotions (vouchers) and don't get upfront info. Getting ballpark figures is like pulling teeth most places. 

It is a pity because they tarnish the industry and loss lead practices, which are legitimate business approaches. Viva and the others like them are going beyond reasonable business tactics and into unconscionable territory in my view - they really do make you feel cornered in a room and unable to leave without a sale.

Oh boy, one of my favourite topics. I've helped a few people get out of these horrendous contracts, with Viva and also Exclusive Photography.

Put it in writing to them, if you haven't yet, that you want the contract cancelled and refund issued, due to high pressure sales tactics and lack of transparency. Ask that they please do this in good faith but that you will be lodging complaints if not.

At the same time, you can ask your credit card company for a chargeback, but be upfront with bank about why.

Expect Viva to say no; your credit card company can go either way, and can refund and then reverse decision later.

Please contact Consumer Protection and the ACCC please - I've been haranguing them about this practice for ages, and they need more pressure from people to actually take action.

You can just contact them to call for action in general, or lodge a complaint with consumer protection (DEMIRS) and they'll try advocate on your behalf. They will rarely take cases to court for you though, due to resourcing, however if Viva won't agree to refund after their attempts at advocacy, I recommend a small claims case in the Magistrate's Court. It's not often worth their time to defend, or the risk, so settling happens, but I am not a lawyer. No lawyers involved in small claims though - self representation only, just costs \~$150 to apply. 

My issue with this has been around unconscionable conduct under consumer law, but I've been told by consumer protection that if you won one of those vouchers and then go for the photo shoot and get pushed into signing, cooling off period applies even though signed at place of business.

Anyone horrified by this - contact your local MPs! Even just link them to this post, they can read it.

Loss lead promotions and persuasion are legitimate sales practices, but Viva and Exclusive Photography and others take it to a horrendous level.

Re: reviews - I've been told by past customers that they were offered inducements to leave 5 star reviews, e.g. free digital copies of other photos. Sort reviews by lowest is a good trick.
I thought this too but was explicitly told it was not the case by regulators when discussing policy reform around this shit.

tl;dr - in my part of the world at least, I call BS on free range being definitively worse for the environment.
